hops.title: Mumbai: approval of a negotiated bid
hops.summary: Home Department approved GVPR appointment at ₹2,098.92 crore including GST on 15 April 2026; GR directs subsequent work-order action. It is not payment.

sourceLocators.locator: GR CCT-3125; PDF pp.2–4

hops.dateBasis: Dated disclosure; exact event or snapshot is stated in the summary.
hops.response: The GR describes four bids, two technically qualified bidders and a negotiated QCBS H1 approval. It directs subsequent work-order action; no payment or duplicate billing is established.
alternatives: The disclosed arrangement can be lawful; a document gap does not establish misconduct.
hops.missingNextDocument: Executed work order, stage invoices, acceptance certificates and treasury/bank payment advice
hops.documentHolder: Maharashtra Home Department / Mumbai Police procurement office
limitations: Four bids and two qualified bidders; QCBS H1 is not generic price L1.

hops.title: Why PFC is a public-sector connection
hops.summary: PFC’s own presentation identifies 55.99% held by the President of India institutionally at 30 June 2025. This adds a public ownership layer; it does not show ministerial direction of the loan.

sourceLocators.locator: PDF p.4: majority owned by Government of India; p.26: shareholder outlook as of 30 June 2025

hops.dateBasis: Dated disclosure; exact event or snapshot is stated in the summary.
hops.response: PFC reports 55.99% institutional government ownership at 30 June 2025. This is not a personal asset of the President or evidence of political direction of this loan.
alternatives: The disclosed arrangement can be lawful; a document gap does not establish misconduct.
hops.missingNextDocument: None required for this dated ownership fact; a loan decision would need its own approval record
limitations: Not the personal shareholding of the President; no sovereign guarantee or political instruction inferred.

hops.title: Policy change: port lending is within the disclosed expansion
hops.summary: PFC’s FY 2022–23 Board report says Government of India approved logistics/infrastructure lending in August 2022 and describes entry into ports. This challenges a sector-name-only diversion theory.

sourceLocators.locator: PDF p.1, printed annual-report p.42, section 1(i)

hops.dateBasis: Approval month August 2022, reported in FY 2022–23 Board report; no exact event day asserted.
hops.financialStage: Dated policy-scope context; no loan payment
hops.response: PFC’s Board explicitly says government approved infrastructure lending in August 2022 and describes lending to ports. Sector diversification alone therefore does not show misuse of power-sector funds.
alternatives: The disclosed arrangement can be lawful; a document gap does not establish misconduct.
hops.missingNextDocument: Underlying government approval, operative MoA and loan-specific eligibility review
limitations: A general lending-scope expansion does not establish that an individual loan complied with all conditions.

hypotheses.question: Which disclosed cash sources funded the port contribution, and did PFC subsequently disburse?
hypotheses.observation: A ₹79.48 crore aggregate contribution is disclosed while PFC debt remained undrawn at the snapshot.
hypotheses.disconfirmationTest: A contributor-resolved funding ledger reconciled to lawful cash balances and bank advice can establish ordinary financing; absence of any CCTV receipts would defeat that proposed upstream route.
limitations: This is a testable review question; missing documents and network proximity do not establish wrongdoing.

hypotheses.question: Did actual DDF payments respect the contracted service-level and milestone conditions?
hypotheses.observation: The rating describes a consumer-payment priority mechanism and authority-related execution delays.
expectedDocumentaryFootprints: Approved invoices, deductions and grant-release statements
hypotheses.disconfirmationTest: Reconcile aggregated DDF inflows to approved bills, SLA performance, penalties and funds released; compliant receipts and deductions would refute leakage.
neededRecords: Approved invoices, deductions and grant-release statements
limitations: This is a testable review question; missing documents and network proximity do not establish wrongdoing.

hypotheses.question: Can either bond batch be connected to a specific legal contractor and a particular procurement cash receipt?
hypotheses.observation: Serial matches identify two party recipients, but purchaser legal identity and upstream account transactions are missing.
expectedDocumentaryFootprints: Specified procurement payment and decision record
hypotheses.disconfirmationTest: Reject the bridge if registered identity or audited donor disclosure differs. Even a valid identity match does not prove exchange: reconcile original cash sources and decision records; date proximity alone is insufficient.

limitations: This is a testable review question; missing documents and network proximity do not establish wrongdoing.
